---
title: "Statistics and probability"
subtitle: "Random variables, conditioning, and limit theorems"
---

Probability is a calculus of uncertainty with a measure underneath.
Statistics is the inverse problem: data in, statements about a
mechanism out. This page keeps the two in one place so the
vocabulary stays aligned.

## Probability, as a machine {#sec-prob}

A probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ is the stage.
A **random variable** is a measurable map $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$
(or $\mathbb R^d$). The law of $X$ is the push-forward
$\mathbb P\circ X^{-1}$.

Working objects:

- **Expectation** $\mathbb E[X]$ as an integral; linearity does
  not need independence.
- **Variance** as the $L^2$ distance to the mean.
- **Independence** as factorisation of joint laws (or of
  $\sigma$-algebras).
- **Conditioning** as “restrict, then renormalise”:
  $\mathbb P(A\mid B) = \mathbb P(A\cap B)/\mathbb P(B)$ when
  $\mathbb P(B)>0$, and the conditional-expectation version
  when $B$ is a $\sigma$-algebra.

Bayes' theorem is that last idea written for a parameter and a
likelihood.

## The usual limit theorems {#sec-limits}

Three statements do most of the daily work.

1. **Law of large numbers.** Sample means converge (in probability,
   or almost surely) to $\mathbb E[X]$ when the mean exists.
2. **Central limit theorem.** Fluctuations of the mean, after
   $\sqrt n$ scaling, become Gaussian under a second-moment
   hypothesis.
3. **Concentration.** Tail bounds (Hoeffding, Bernstein, …) when
   you need finite-$n$ control, not only an asymptotic shape.

These are analysis theorems about measures. The
[analysis page](../analysis/calculus-and-complex.qmd) is where
characteristic functions and inversion live.

## Statistics, as inverse probability {#sec-stats}

A **model** is a family of laws $\{P_\theta\}$. Data $x$ is treated
as a realisation of $X\sim P_\theta$. Standard jobs:

| Job | Typical object |
|-----|----------------|
| Point estimate | MLE, method of moments, Bayes posterior mean |
| Interval | Confidence set or credible set |
| Test | $H_0$ versus $H_1$; $p$-value as a tail of a null |
| Prediction | A law for a new $X$, not only for $\theta$ |

Linear models later reuse
[matrix decompositions](../linear-algebra/matrix-decompositions.qmd)
(QR for least squares, SVD for PCA, Cholesky for covariances).

## Dynamic modelling {#sec-dynamic}

Markov chains are the simplest dynamics with noise: the next state
depends on the present, not on the path that got you there. They
are classified by time (discrete or continuous), by the size of the
state space, by transition structure (absorbing, irreducible,
ergodic), and by whether the state is observed. The types overlap:
a discrete-time chain can also be finite and absorbing. Hidden
Markov models keep the chain latent and emit observations.
